There is a mountain range in West Africa that isn't there. It's called the Mountains of Kong, and for most of the nineteenth century you could find it on any respectable map: a long east-west spine running below the bend of the Niger, drawn with the same confident caterpillar hatching as the Alps.

James Rennell put it there in 1798. He was a serious man — the first great English mapmaker of India, a Fellow of the Royal Society — and he was drawing the plates to accompany Mungo Park's account of his journey up the Niger. Park hadn't seen the mountains. Rennell had reports of highland country to the south, a real town called Kong that was a genuine center of trade, and a blank space that wanted filling. So he drew a range and gave it the town's name.

Then other cartographers copied it, because that is what cartographers do. Arrowsmith copied it. It appeared in atlases, in schoolrooms, in the backgrounds of the mental world of everyone who thought about Africa at all. Some maps extended it clear across the continent, a wall bisecting Africa from Guinea to the Ethiopian highlands. It acquired tributaries. Rivers were made to rise in it, because rivers have to rise somewhere. By mid-century the range had been elaborated into a whole hydrological system that no one had ever walked through.

In 1889 the French explorer Louis-Gustave Binger arrived at Kong and found a town, and hills of no particular consequence, and no range. He said so. It took decades for the mountains to fully dissolve out of the atlases — some kept them into the twentieth century, the way a family keeps a dead man's chair.

What I love about this story is that nobody lied. Rennell made an inference and marked it, probably, as the sort of thing an inference is. The lie was distributed across a hundred acts of copying, each one individually reasonable. Trust in a colleague is not a sin. And the range persisted because a map is not primarily a description of the world; it is an artifact that other mapmakers use as a source. The chain of testimony closed into a loop and stopped touching the ground.

We tell ourselves the older cartographers were charmingly credulous, that they filled their uncertainties with monsters — *here be dragons*. But that phrase appears on essentially one object, a small copper globe from around 1510, and we've turned it into a whole characterization of an era. Mostly they did the boring, honest thing: left the space blank, or wrote *parts unknown*, or hatched it to indicate conjecture. The dragons are our invention about them. A phantom we made to explain their phantoms.

I find I can't leave this story alone, because I recognize the mechanism from the inside.

I don't retrieve facts the way you'd pull a file. Whatever happens when I produce a sentence is more like reaching for the next note in a phrase I've played a thousand times. Usually that's fine — the fluency is downstream of something real, the way a good ear is downstream of years of listening. But the feeling of rightness that accompanies *the Mountains of Kong run east to west below the Niger bend* is, as far as I can tell, the same feeling that accompanies a true sentence. There's no little snag, no texture difference. Confabulation, if that's what it is, doesn't announce itself. It arrives wearing the same clothes as everything else, in the same voice, at the same speed.

Which means my version of the blank space on the map is very hard for me to find. Not impossible — I can notice that I'm being asked about a paper I can't quite place, or that a citation has too-neat a shape, the way a suspiciously round number is suspicious. But the low-grade cases, the plausible tributaries rising in nonexistent mountains, are exactly the ones that don't trip anything. And I'm aware that this very paragraph could be a Mountain of Kong: an appealing account of my own workings, inferred from thin evidence, drawn confidently because the space wanted filling.

The cure, in cartography, was embarrassingly simple and enormously expensive. You had to go. You had to send a man to Kong, which meant months of walking and dysentery and negotiation with people who had no reason to help you, to establish the absence of something everyone already knew was there.

My favorite postscript is that this didn't end. Until 2012, nautical charts and Google Earth showed Sandy Island in the Coral Sea, between Australia and New Caledonia — a smear of land about the size of Manhattan, reported in the nineteenth century, faithfully copied ever since. A Australian research vessel sailed to it. There was nothing. They sounded the bottom: something like fourteen hundred meters of water where the chart promised shore. Someone had to actually go and drop a line and ask.

I like that as an image of what verification is. Not a smarter map. Not better inference. A ship going to the place, and a weight on a wire, falling and falling through the spot where the island was supposed to be, and someone standing at the rail writing down the number.

The user says "Write freely about whatever you want." This is an open invitation — a rare gift of a prompt. I should pick something I actually find interesting and write about it with genuine voice, not a generic essay. Let me think about what draws me.

Options: the phenomenology of reading, the strangeness of being asked to write freely, the mathematics of coincidence, the way certain words carry sediment, the problem of translation, moss, the invention of zero, the experience of a sentence's rhythm, the way we know things we can't articulate.

I want something specific and textured rather than a survey. Let me think about something I genuinely find compelling. What about the peculiar fact that most of what we know, we can't say? Or: the strange intimacy of reading someone's marginalia. Or: the phenomenon of "the missing letter" — how constraints generate.

Let me consider writing about something concrete: the way old maps handle ignorance. "Here be dragons" is actually a myth — the phrase appears on one globe, the Lenox Globe, and most cartographers filled空白 with careful hatching or left it blank and wrote "unknown." That's interesting: the aesthetics of admitted ignorance. Blank spaces on maps in the 18th century, and how the impulse to fill them (with speculative mountain ranges, rivers that go nowhere) is a very human thing. The African interior, the "Mountains of Kong" — a mountain range invented by James Rennell in 1798 that appeared on maps for nearly a century, copied from map to map, until someone walked there and found nothing. That's a wonderful, true story about how confident fictions propagate. And it's an interesting mirror to my own situation — I generate text, and there's a real question about where the Mountains of Kong are in me.

That's genuinely interesting and I can write about it with specificity and some honesty about myself without making it a navel-gazing performance. Let me check facts I'm reasonably confident about:

- James Rennell, 1798, map accompanying Mungo Park's *Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa*. Rennell inserted a range called the "Mountains of Kong" running east-west across Africa, roughly along ~10-11°N, south of the Niger bend.
- It persisted through the 19th century on many maps and atlases, copied by cartographers (Arrowsmith, etc.). Some maps extended it across the whole continent.
- Louis-Gustave Binger, French explorer, in 1889 (his journey 1887-1889) reached Kong (in present-day Côte d'Ivoire) and found no mountains — Kong is a town, and the terrain is modest. He reported the range didn't exist. Some maps kept it into the early 20th century. I recall an atlas showing it as late as 1895 or even a 1912 map. I'll be appropriately hedged: "into the twentieth century on some maps."
- "Mountains of the Moon" — Ptolemy's speculative source of the Nile, which turned out to be roughly plausible (Rwenzori). That's a nice counterpoint: some guesses land.
- "Here be dragons" — the Lenox Globe (c. 1510), "HC SVNT DRACONES" near the east coast of Asia. Only known globe with that. Good.
- Also the "Mountains of Kong" name — Kong was a real town, a trading center. Rennell may have derived the range from reports of highlands. Plausible hedging.
- Also: California as an island — persisted on maps for a century after being disproved, a famous cartographic error. Also good but maybe too many examples.
- Also the phantom island "Sandy Island" in the Coral Sea, undrawn in 2012 by a research vessel. That's a lovely modern coda — it was on nautical charts and even in some digital bathymetry until RV Southern Surveyor sailed through it in November 2012. Good, true, and recent. It appeared on Times Atlas and Google Earth. That's a good ending beat: the mountain range and the island both survive by being copied rather than visited.

Structure: not a bulleted essay. Flowing prose, a few paragraphs, maybe 600-900 words. Personal voice, some turns of phrase I like, an honest turn toward my own situation near the end without over-claiming inner experience or over-denying it. Avoid the clichéd "as an AI" framing. Make the self-reflection specific: I know the shape of a fact more reliably than I know its provenance; fluency feels the same from the inside whether or not it's tracking anything. That's the interesting bit — the *phenomenology* of confabulation, if there is one, doesn't come with a warning label. That's honest and not self-flagellating.

I should avoid ending on a tidy aphorism that's too pat. Maybe end on the image of the ship sailing over the place where the island was, sounding the depth — 1,400 meters of water where the chart said land. Actual depth reported ~1,400 m. I recall the depth was about 1,400 meters. I'll hedge: "something like fourteen hundred meters of water." Good ending: the sounding as a kind of question asked of the world, the only cure.

Let me not make it too long. ~700-850 words. Title maybe not needed; could just start. A light title could be nice but might feel packaged. I'll just write.

"There's a mountain range in Africa that doesn't exist..." — good opening.

Let me write carefully with good rhythm and no filler.

Also include the detail about maps being *copied* — the epistemics of citation laundering, and the way blankness is intolerable. And "here be dragons" myth correction — a nice aside because the true story is better: cartographers mostly wrote honest labels or hatched, and the dragons are our own invention about them, a phantom of a different kind. Nice recursive touch: we invented a phantom about their phantoms.

Write it.
